title: Grim Reach Idle: Released 3 Months Ago, Now I Have Players With 1000h+ Played Time On Steam.
author: Shalke97
selftext:
Hey everyone,

By now, some of you might recognize me or my game. I'm the solo developer behind **Grim Reach Idle (https://store.steampowered.com/app/4915450/Grim\_Reach\_Idle/)** , a (currently) singleplayer, scape-like dark fantasy idle RPG. What a tongue twister! I'm a software developer from germany and have only been developing games for a few months now. You read that right, i actually created a game, with the help of AI, that keeps players around for hundreds (now thousands!) of hours. You could argue "That's only because it's an idler" and yes, that's fair, but it's still a great achievement in my book!

**First of all, thank you**

I just want to thank everybody who gave my game a shot. I feel incredibly privileged to be able to say that my game has reached this amount of success. Some might think it's small or meaningless, but for my first release, this absolutely blew past my expectations. I poured my heart and soul into designing the perfect idler for myself, the way i wanted it to be. Seeing other people enjoy that is honestly a little hard to put into words. So sincerely, thank you, from the bottom of my heart. You're fulfilling this man-child's dream :)

I also wanted to share some of the things i learned while developing Grim Reach Idle and keeping it running after release.

**"How did you market your game?"**

This is the question i get the most. Honestly, this is my weakest skill by far, probably like many of us. I didn't really market my game at all. I put it up, waited until i could release it and... i just did. No planning, i didn't look at the wishlists, i honestly didn't care at the time. All i wanted was to make a good game and see if it reached the right people.

Does that mean you should do it the same way? Absolutely not. With what i know now about wishlists, conversion rates and all that, i'd say wishlists are very important to give your game a chance of getting noticed by the algorithm. What i'm trying to say is: don't stress so much about wishlists and numbers that you lose sight of making a good game you're proud of.

**Project scope**

Another problem i see here all the time. Alot of posts here are about projects that seem way too big for a single developer. And you might say "But you can't know if that's too much for someone!" You're right, i can't. But i do think a lot of people will burn out before they even finish half of what they planned. If you're making your first game, do something simpler. Ask yourself: "Do i have the tools and skills to take this game from 0 to 100?" And if the answer is no, start smaller.

I would love to make a 3D RPG in my own universe. Who wouldn't? But do i have reliable tools to make everything that would need? Not yet. 3D is still iffy with AI, and animations can be quirky if you aren't using pre-made assets. Having 5–6 nice Meshy models is cool, but can you REALLY scale that up to hundreds of NPCs? Will they look good together? Will the rigging work properly? Those are things you need to figure out before you've already sunk months into it. Do something simple so you can learn the fundamentals of good game design. Focus less on pretty graphics, try finding your own artstyle and make something that feels like yours.

**The last 10% are the hardest**

This is so disgustingly true that i want to throw up. I have three games in development, with Grim Reach Idle being the only one released so far, and i've felt this with every project. You'll chew away at those last 10% for weeks and months on end. Thats why i really recommend building your game in a way that makes things easy to revisit and change. Good architecture matters a lot, especially when you're working with AI and paying for token usage. You'll be coming back to things more often than you think.

**And to everyone who needs to hear it: don't give up**

Don't do this just for money or fame. You need passion, and you need to believe in what you're making. Keep learning, try to get better and push yourself to build something you're happy with. For me, making games used to be one of those things i'd dream about without knowing how to actually do it. Now i've released one, and people are spending their time playing it. That still feels a bit unreal. There are so many creative people who have ideas but were missing the skills to bring them to life. Being able to finally do that means a lot to me, and i'm sure i'm not the only one.

And fuck all the Anti-AI shit going on :-)

\- Adhavar

comments.author: _kevurugames
comments.body: The part about scope really hits home. Getting a game released is already a huge achievement, but keeping it updated and improving it afterward is a whole different challenge. I also agree that AI can help you get started, but you still need to make the design decisions and put in the work to make the game actually fun. Congrats on the milestone!

replies.author: Shalke97
replies.body: Thank you! Yes i faced the scope problem myself on other projects i was or i am working on currently. Everytime i think "this is a reasonable scope to actually get done." but in the end, its always 5-10x the amount of work.

comments.author: randommmoso
comments.body: without sounding rude I looked at your trailer and I didn't see a gameplay? it's just glorified Claude code excel with super bad assets and no game at all? Where is the actual combat taking place? Don't tell me that super awkward animation of your hero "hitting" to the right and monster "hitting" to the left is all there is to it?

replies.author: Shalke97
replies.body: Hey, feel free to look at the Idler Genre in general, like Melvor Idle for instance. Maybe you'll get a grasp of how these games work! And yes, trailers are always the wonkiest thing to get right for an Idler since there is not much "action gameplay" you can show. I'm already working on something better :)
